title: Peter Claver (1580–1654)
hookLine: in Cartagena he met every slave ship and called himself the slave of the slaves

lines: PEOPLE IN CHAINS IN THE HOLD.
cards: Word comes into the port of Cartagena that a ship has been sighted. For the merchants, that means cargo.
For the people in the hold, it means the end of a voyage they were forced to make in chains, sick, starving, some of them dying.

And for one Spanish Jesuit, it means going down to the docks with baskets of food, water, lemons and medicine, and climbing down into the hold. This is a hard story, and it should be told plainly. Today, Peter Claver.

teach.b: First, the place. Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of what is now Colombia, was a port where enslaved Africans were brought and sold. Claver was sent there as a young man.
Before he left Spain, an elderly Jesuit brother, Alphonsus Rodriguez, a doorkeeper, had urged him toward the people no one cared for. Second, the docks. When a ship came in, Claver went below decks.
He brought food and water first, and washed and bandaged the sick. He used interpreters to speak to people in their own languages, and taught and baptized those who asked.
He followed them into the yards where they were held, and later to plantations and hospitals. Third, the vow.
At his final vows as a Jesuit, he signed his name with a Latin phrase: the slave of the Africans forever. It passed down as slave of the slaves. Fourth, the honest part.
Claver didn't end the slave trade, and the Church of his day did not condemn it outright.

teach.h: HE COULDN'T STOP IT. HE SERVED.
teach.b: He served inside an evil he could not stop, and those who tell his story now try to remember both: his love, and the system it ran into.

teach.h: I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU GAVE ME TO EAT.
teach.b: Jesus's words in Matthew read like his job description, in the Douay-Rheims: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty, and you gave me to drink."
Near the end Claver was sick and largely forgotten, poorly cared for himself. The Church later named him a saint, and Catholics invoke him as a patron of enslaved people.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Peter Claver and invoke him as a patron of enslaved people and of ministry to African-descended communities; some parishes mark it with prayer for victims of human trafficking.

games.q: you're Claver. a slave ship has just docked, and the people below are sick and starving. what do you bring down first?
games.why: he brought food, water and medicine first, washed the sick, and only then taught those who asked.

practice: Forced labor didn't end with the ships: people are still trafficked, held in debt, made to work without pay or freedom, sometimes close to where you live.

Let them be present, without names, the way the people in the hold were present to Claver. If you pray, ask Peter Claver to pray for them, or pray an Our Father slowly; if not, simply stay with them, and let it cost you a little.

wordCard.voice: Peter Claver. A Spanish Jesuit in Cartagena who met the slave ships with food and medicine, and called himself the slave of the Africans forever.

orig.note: Latin: 'slave of the Africans forever', the phrase Claver signed with his final vows (aethiops was the old Latin word for an African).

carryVoice: Your line: slave of the slaves. He went down into the hold when others stayed on the dock. Until tomorrow.
